### Wool Crochet (`lumenary:wool-crochet`, models this process)

_From: Hooked yarn craft; when: Printed patterns from the 1820s; works best on: Bold shapes and few colours._

Crochet builds cloth one loop at a time with a single hook, and every stitch shows. A picture in crochet is a grid, like knitting, but the stitches are chunkier, each row is worked in the opposite direction to the last, and the edge is usually finished with a decorative border. The charm is in the slight unevenness of something made by hand.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Average the picture to one colour per stitch.
2. Find a few wool colours and give each stitch the nearest one.
3. Draw each stitch as two strands leaning into a V, each with a shadow and a highlight.
4. Shift every second row by half a stitch and reverse the overlap of its strands.
5. Work a border of shells, five stitches fanned from one foot.
6. Add a little fuzz: fine noise and the odd stray fibre.

**The maths:**

$$w=\frac{W-2e}{n},\qquad \text{rows}=\operatorname{round}\!\Big(\frac{H-2e}{0.86\,w}\Big)$$

_Stitch width w from n stitches across and the border width e. Stitches are a little shorter than wide._ (primitives: stitch-grid)

$$\text{strand}:\ (0.22w,\ 0.1h)\to(0.5w,\ 0.92h),\qquad (0.78w,\ 0.1h)\to(0.5w,\ 0.92h)$$

_The two strands of one stitch, in a cell w wide and h tall. Line width is 0.36 w._ (primitives: stitch-grid)

$$\theta_q=(q-2)\cdot0.42\ \text{rad},\qquad q=0,\dots,4$$

_The five stitches of one shell, fanned about its foot._ (primitives: stitch-grid)

**Dials:** `stitches` (Stitches across) = 46 [24 to 90]; `colours` (Balls of wool) = 7 [3 to 10]; `fuzz` (Fuzz) = 50 [0 to 100]; `wool` (Wool) = "own" (own, pastel, earth); `border` (Shell border) = true; `seed` (Start again) = 1.

**History:** Crochet as we know it appears in Europe in the early nineteenth century; the Dutch magazine Penélopé printed patterns in 1823. In Ireland during the famine of the 1840s, crocheted lace became a cottage industry that fed families. The granny square, made from leftover yarn, spread in the twentieth century, and Japan’s amigurumi, small crocheted creatures, made the craft popular with a new generation.
